ann_85.original: Linear backbone: each input's own edge into the score, in logit per sd of the input. The largest direct weights are day charge 2.83, voice-mail plan -1.24, evening charge 0.95, international plan 0.84, evening minutes 0.42, night charge 0.32, international charge 0.31, day minutes 0.27, voicemail messages 0.20, international calls -0.19 and account length 0.14; the state indicators add small per-state offsets. Several of these inputs also feed hidden parts, so the whole-model effect differs from the direct weight. Day and evening usage: the day-usage hinge cancels most of these steep direct slopes for lighter users (see day_eve_hinge). International plan: direct weight 0.84 per sd; in the whole model, giving the typical customer a plan moves predicted risk from 4% to 35%; the 380 plan holders in training churn at 42.4% with mean predicted risk 42.2%. Voice-mail plan: direct weight -1.24 per sd; in the whole model the plan moves the typical customer from 4% to 1% and a heavy day user (300 minutes) from 83% to 23%. The protection is larger in logit for the heavy user because at typical usage the plan also raises the hinge unit (from 1.46 to 2.72), which gives part of the direct effect back, while for the heavy user the hinge is off (0.00). Replacing every direct term by its training mean lowers training AUC from 0.917 to 0.400.
ann_85.proposed: This part weighs each input on its own: through it, higher total daytime charge raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves steadily, an international plan raises it, and a voice-mail plan lowers it.

ann_86.original: Usage-level switch. For customers without an international plan it is off at or below 160 day minutes and on at or above 165: in training, 0 no-plan customers at or below 160 minutes have it on and 0 no-plan customers at or above 165 minutes have it off; it is off for 1282 customers (the no-plan customers at or below 160 minutes, 1282 rows with the switch off in all). An international plan keeps it on (0 plan holders have it off). Its own edges to the output are small (-0.042 and -0.021 per unit). Its main job is to veto the service-call escalation: for a 130-minute customer with 5 calls the escalation unit is 0.87 without a plan and 0.00 with one, and at 250 minutes without a plan it is 0.00. In a day-minutes sweep without a plan the switch is 0.00 at 160 minutes and 0.18 at 165. Setting the part to its baseline (gated exits off) lowers training AUC from 0.917 to 0.909.
ann_86.proposed: Through this part, the predicted chance that a customer leaves goes down once total daytime minutes rise above about 142 minutes, in an uneven way (for 380 of the 4000 training customers it already changes below that), and an international plan lowers it.

ann_89.original: Service-call escalation for low-usage customers. When the usage-level switch is off, the escalation unit fires from 3 customer-service calls: among customers with the switch off, 0 with 3 or more calls have it silent, and 0 customers with fewer than 3 calls have it firing. It fires for 306 training customers (46 of them with the switch weakly on, at high call counts); their churn rate is 35.9% and their mean predicted risk 39.8%. The part's two exits feed the day-usage hinge, not the output, so each extra call pushes the hinge further on. In the whole model, for a 130-minute customer without an international plan, predicted risk is 3% at 2 calls, 15% at 3 and 80% at 4 (the service-call term adds to this as well); for a 250-minute customer the escalation stays silent and risk stays at 23% up to 4 calls. The voice-mail plan also enters this part and raises the hinge input (see direct_terms). Holding the part's exits at their training means lowers training AUC from 0.917 to 0.887.
ann_89.proposed: Through this part, a voice-mail plan raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves, and more customer-service calls raise it in an uneven way.

ann_90.original: Day-and-evening usage hinge, the model's main nonlinearity. Through their own edges, day usage (day charge 2.83, day minutes 0.27 per sd) and evening usage (evening charge 0.95, evening minutes 0.42 per sd) push the score up steeply. This unit (output weight 1.31) is on for lighter users and falls as day minutes and evening charge rise, so it cancels most of those slopes: predicted risk stays flat for ordinary usage and climbs once combined day and evening usage passes the point where the unit switches off. In probes of the typical customer with day charge moved with day minutes, predicted risk is 4% at 100 minutes, 3% at 150, 5% at 200, 23% at 250 and 83% at 300; the unit is 0.73 at 200 minutes and 0.00 at 250. Evening usage matters little for light day users: moving evening minutes (and charge) from 150 to 250 changes risk from 3% to 3% at 150 day minutes, but from 55% to 95% at 300. The unit is off for 847 training customers, who churn at 32.9% (mean predicted 33.3%), against 9.1% for the 3153 with it on. Its third input, from the service-call escalation, keeps it on (and growing) for low-usage customers with many calls, which is how the escalation raises their risk. Switching the unit off lowers training AUC from 0.917 to 0.773.
ann_90.proposed: This part gives lighter daytime users a higher predicted chance of leaving: through it, higher total daytime minutes lower the predicted chance steadily up to about 230 minutes (between 188 minutes and 275 minutes for different customers), then no further.

ann_91.original: Light-day-user dampener. The unit is on for 1429 training customers with low day minutes and lowers the score through a negative output weight (-0.136 per unit); for the customers it acts on, its mean contribution is -0.184 logit. In a day-minutes sweep it contributes -0.002 at 160 minutes and 0.000 at 165; in the typical-customer probes (day charge moved with minutes) it contributes -0.31 at 100 minutes and -0.05 at 150, making the lightest users slightly safer and partly offsetting the rise the day hinge gives them at the low end. It barely matters for ranking: switching it off moves training AUC from 0.9174 to 0.9164. Described more than explained: a small correction to the day-usage curve.
ann_91.proposed: Through this part, higher total daytime minutes raise the predicted chance that a customer leaves steadily up to about 160 minutes, then no further, so it lowers the predicted chance for the lightest daytime users.

ann_92.original: Service-call term, damped by day spending and in three states. Many customer-service calls raise the score through this part (output weight 1.73); for light day spenders the rise starts at 3 calls, for heavy day spenders it starts later. With an international plan at 130 minutes (escalation silent) the unit is 0.22 at 2 calls and 1.94 at 5, and predicted risk goes from 32% to 90%; at 250 minutes without a plan the unit is 0.00 at 4 calls and 0.44 at 5, and risk goes from 23% at 4 calls to 85% at 7. Light day spenders carry a small term even without calls (unit 0.22 at 0 calls and 130 minutes). Three states get a smaller term: at 5 calls and 130 minutes the unit is 1.94 in West Virginia but 0.70 in Michigan (80 training customers), 0.00 in Nebraska (72) and 0.22 in New Jersey (90); these look fitted to those few customers. The unit is on for 1348 training customers, with a mean contribution of 1.02 logit for them. Switching it off lowers training AUC from 0.917 to 0.898.
ann_92.proposed: Through this part, customer-service calls add to the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 3 calls upwards (between 2 calls and 5 calls for different customers), in an uneven way; for 1877 of the 4000 training customers it already changes below that. Higher total daytime charge lowers it steadily up to about 25.13 US dollars (between 25.13 US dollars and 31.31 US dollars for different customers), then no further (for 794 of the 4000 training customers it still changes above that), and in Michigan and Nebraska the part adds less.

Through this part, the typical customer (West Virginia) gets -0.26 logit relative to the part's mean; Missouri gets -0.90, Massachusetts -0.52, New York -0.42, Florida -0.34, Texas -0.16 and Michigan 0.00; area code 408 gets -0.35 against -0.26 for 415. In the whole model (each state's direct edge included) this moves the typical customer's predicted risk from 4% to 2% in Missouri (80 training customers) and 5% in Michigan (80). ann_94.original: How the four usage parts combine. Serially, the usage-level switch inhibits the service-call escalation, and the escalation feeds the day-and-evening hinge; in parallel, the hinge, the low-day dampener and the usage switch's small direct edges feed the output. Net effect: predicted risk is flat for ordinary usage, climbs steeply for heavy day and evening users, and climbs steeply with calls for low-usage customers without an international plan, so the call count can reverse the usage ordering. Self-probe, in the whole model: at 2 calls the 130-minute and 250-minute customers (no plan) have predicted risk 3% and 23%; at 4 calls, 80% and 23%. Customers with the switch off and 3 or more calls (260) churn at 36.2% (mean predicted 39.4%). Setting the whole engine to its baseline lowers training AUC from 0.917 to 0.778.
ann_94.proposed: Through this part, higher total daytime minutes and higher total evening charge lower the predicted chance that a customer leaves, each in an uneven way. Through it, a voice-mail plan raises the predicted chance, and higher daytime minutes raise it more without a voice-mail plan, in a curve that is lowest at about 110 minutes and higher either side.

Training AUC is 0.917. The call counts, night minutes, international minutes, area code 510 and several states are not connected to the network and do not affect the prediction.

parts.name: churn_model
parts.original_hypothesis: Churn score: the direct terms, the day-usage engine, the service-call term and the state offsets are added on the log-odds scale and passed through a sigmoid. The model predicts high churn risk for heavy day and evening users, for customers with many customer-service calls (strongest for low-usage customers without an international plan), and for international plan holders; a voice-mail plan lowers risk. Its subgroup predictions track the training outcome: customers above 250 day minutes (393) churn at 48.9% against a mean predicted 47.3%; customers with 4 or more calls (318) at 50.0% against 48.3%; plan holders (380) at 42.4% against 42.2%; voice-mail plan holders (1061) at 7.4% against 8.2%. Training AUC is 0.917. The call counts, night minutes, international minutes, area code 510 and several states are not connected to the network and do not affect the prediction.

parts.name: direct_terms
parts.original_hypothesis: Linear backbone: each input's own edge into the score, in logit per sd of the input. The largest direct weights are day charge 2.83, voice-mail plan -1.24, evening charge 0.95, international plan 0.84, evening minutes 0.42, night charge 0.32, international charge 0.31, day minutes 0.27, voicemail messages 0.20, international calls -0.19 and account length 0.14; the state indicators add small per-state offsets. Several of these inputs also feed hidden parts, so the whole-model effect differs from the direct weight. Day and evening usage: the day-usage hinge cancels most of these steep direct slopes for lighter users (see day_eve_hinge). International plan: direct weight 0.84 per sd; in the whole model, giving the typical customer a plan moves predicted risk from 4% to 35%; the 380 plan holders in training churn at 42.4% with mean predicted risk 42.2%. Voice-mail plan: direct weight -1.24 per sd; in the whole model the plan moves the typical customer from 4% to 1% and a heavy day user (300 minutes) from 83% to 23%. The protection is larger in logit for the heavy user because at typical usage the plan also raises the hinge unit (from 1.46 to 2.72), which gives part of the direct effect back, while for the heavy user the hinge is off (0.00). Replacing every direct term by its training mean lowers training AUC from 0.917 to 0.400.

parts.name: day_eve_hinge
parts.original_hypothesis: Day-and-evening usage hinge, the model's main nonlinearity. Through their own edges, day usage (day charge 2.83, day minutes 0.27 per sd) and evening usage (evening charge 0.95, evening minutes 0.42 per sd) push the score up steeply. This unit (output weight 1.31) is on for lighter users and falls as day minutes and evening charge rise, so it cancels most of those slopes: predicted risk stays flat for ordinary usage and climbs once combined day and evening usage passes the point where the unit switches off. In probes of the typical customer with day charge moved with day minutes, predicted risk is 4% at 100 minutes, 3% at 150, 5% at 200, 23% at 250 and 83% at 300; the unit is 0.73 at 200 minutes and 0.00 at 250. Evening usage matters little for light day users: moving evening minutes (and charge) from 150 to 250 changes risk from 3% to 3% at 150 day minutes, but from 55% to 95% at 300. The unit is off for 847 training customers, who churn at 32.9% (mean predicted 33.3%), against 9.1% for the 3153 with it on. Its third input, from the service-call escalation, keeps it on (and growing) for low-usage customers with many calls, which is how the escalation raises their risk. Switching the unit off lowers training AUC from 0.917 to 0.773.

parts.name: day_usage_engine
parts.original_hypothesis: How the four usage parts combine. Serially, the usage-level switch inhibits the service-call escalation, and the escalation feeds the day-and-evening hinge; in parallel, the hinge, the low-day dampener and the usage switch's small direct edges feed the output. Net effect: predicted risk is flat for ordinary usage, climbs steeply for heavy day and evening users, and climbs steeply with calls for low-usage customers without an international plan, so the call count can reverse the usage ordering. Self-probe, in the whole model: at 2 calls the 130-minute and 250-minute customers (no plan) have predicted risk 3% and 23%; at 4 calls, 80% and 23%. Customers with the switch off and 3 or more calls (260) churn at 36.2% (mean predicted 39.4%). Setting the whole engine to its baseline lowers training AUC from 0.917 to 0.778.

When the usage-level switch is off, the escalation unit fires from 3 customer-service calls: among customers with the switch off, 0 with 3 or more calls have it silent, and 0 customers with fewer than 3 calls have it firing. In the whole model, for a 130-minute customer without an international plan, predicted risk is 3% at 2 calls, 15% at 3 and 80% at 4 (the service-call term adds to this as well); for a 250-minute customer the escalation stays silent and risk stays at 23% up to 4 calls. reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient); an input the data ties to a category takes its typical value within that category (linked inputs)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

ann_85.text: Through this part, the model treats a higher total daytime charge as clearly raising the predicted chance that a customer leaves steadily: for a typical customer, it goes from below 1% at 19.07 US dollars to about 68% at 42.40 US dollars (with total daytime minutes at 236 minutes, as in the data), flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher.

Through this part, the model treats a higher total daytime minutes as raising the predicted chance that a customer leaves in an uneven way: for a typical customer, it goes from below 1% at 112 minutes to about 53% at 249 minutes (with total daytime charge at 40.15 US dollars, as in the data), flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower (on the training data only).

Through this part, for a typical customer, the model gives a clearly higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer has an international plan (about 42%) than if the customer has no international plan (about 4%).

Through this part, the model treats a higher total evening minutes as raising the predicted chance that a customer leaves in an uneven way: for a typical customer, it goes from about 1% at 138 minutes to about 26% at 266 minutes (with total evening charge at 24.21 US dollars, as in the data), flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower (on the training data only).

Other effects: a higher total evening charge raises it in an uneven way; California (rather than any other state) raises it; Washington (rather than any other state) raises it; New Jersey (rather than any other state) raises it (on the training data only).

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: a voice-mail plan (rather than no voice-mail plan) lowers it; a higher voice-mail messages lowers it in a curve that is lowest at about 1 messages, higher either side; Hawaii (rather than any other state) lowers it; Vermont (rather than any other state) lowers it; a higher total night-time charge raises it steadily; Colorado (rather than any other state) lowers it; a higher total international charge raises it steadily; Alaska (rather than any other state) lowers it; and 24 still smaller effects listed in the evidence table (on the training data only).
